cards.title: Capital One's move of its debit cards to Discover likely raised merchant interchange on those cards, so each debit cost claim needs scoping by product

observed.text: Trade press reports Capital One has moved about 25 million debit cards onto Discover, and Stripe says those cards are no longer under the Durbin interchange cap.
On a consultancy's quoted rate of 1.10% plus 16 cents, a 50 dollar in-store sale costs 71 cents, against 24.5 cents under the cap.
In 2024 Discover debit averaged 83 cents a transaction, above exempt Visa at 60 and exempt Mastercard at 63, and below both as a share of value.

Stripe told cost-plus users that interchange would likely be higher. It also warned of a one-time rise in card updater fees and possibly lower approvals on unactivated reissues and outside Discover's country coverage.
A merchant services firm says merchants cannot route these cards differently, and that flat-rate or tiered plans bury the new rate in a blended number.
In 2024 PULSE averaged 27 cents a transaction, below Visa and Mastercard dual-message debit at 36 and 43, level with Interlink and above Maestro, STAR and Accel.

inference.text: The study infers that a family-wide lower-cost debit claim would contradict what Stripe and merchant advisers already tell merchants about Capital One debit.
The study infers that acquirers can isolate the change by card range, since migrated cards show under new Discover BINs that advisers already track.

decision.question: How should the acquirer and merchant experience present Discover debit cost now that Capital One's cards carry exempt pricing?
options: Keep a family-wide 'lower cost on debit' claim.
Stay quiet on cost and lead with acceptance, as Discover's debit page does.
Name the change, show it on the acquirer's own data, and scope each cost claim to its product.
decision.evidence_favours: The third, on the study's reading. Per transaction, Discover debit cost more than exempt Visa and Mastercard in 2024 (dgn-077, cross-025). A merchant services firm puts a 50 dollar in-store sale at 2.9 times the cap (dgn-214). Stripe and advisers already tell merchants about the rise (dgn-215, dgn-212). The same firm says flat-rate and tiered plans hide it, and Discover's debit page gives no cost information (dgn-315, dgn-219). Capital One lists a fall in large merchants accepting Discover or PULSE as a material risk (dgn-218). PULSE's 2024 average sat below Visa and Mastercard dual-message debit and level with or above their PIN networks (dgn-076, cross-145, cross-146).

position.text: On merchant cost Discover debit is behind. Its 2024 average per transaction sat above exempt Visa and Mastercard, and its quoted card-present rate sits above Visa's published exempt rate on both terms. PULSE sat below Visa and Mastercard dual-message debit and level with or above their PIN networks.

means.text: Scope each cost claim to the product where it holds, and make no family-wide lower-cost claim on debit. Lead Discover debit for acquirers and merchants with the Capital One cardholders it now carries. Report approvals and disputes as measured results on the acquirer's own traffic.

Rewrite the Debit and ATM card's 'Lower cost on debit' as a measure on Brightline's own debit routes, with no Visa or Mastercard figure. Its price line reads 'Published PULSE schedule', and PULSE publishes no interchange schedule, so that line waits on a business decision to publish. Keep debit interchange out of the cost band, which compares gateway and network fees.

Bayline's Settlement view shows the share of its debit on the new Discover card ranges, what that debit costs and why. Declines on those ranges name their cause, such as an unactivated reissue or a country outside Discover's coverage.
Marcus sees each acquirer's Discover debit share and cost, so he can raise the change with the acquirer first.

objection.text: A Discover executive would say Discover debit took a lower share of value in 2024 than exempt Visa or Mastercard debit, at 1.22% against 1.46% and 1.30%. Capital One told the OCC a three-party system has no interchange to regulate, and that the circumvention charge misrepresents the law. It also said it did not intend to raise fees on its networks as a result of the bank merger.

resolution.text: The share-of-value point holds on its own measure. Per transaction Discover debit averaged 83 cents against 60 and 63, and its quoted card-present rate sits above Visa's published exempt rate on both terms. The OCC pledge is scoped to fees raised as a result of the bank merger, and Stripe ties the rise to the cards leaving the Durbin cap. The product can state the classification plainly and still show each acquirer what its merchants pay.

cards.limit: The Fed's 2024 figures predate the migration, and its table still showed 2024 as the latest year on 26 September 2026 (cross-025, cross-228). Network averages blend pricing programmes and do not show what a given party pays (cross-027). Discover treats its US acquirer fee chart as confidential, so post-migration rates come from merchant advisers (dgn-064, dgn-063, dgn-212). On the consultancy's figures, merchants pay more unless their average in-store ticket is below 5.71 dollars (dgn-213). Capital One told the OCC its debit would be about 6.5% of US debit transactions, and one consultancy assumes about 2% of debit volume (dgn-319, dgn-318). Capital One's 10-K applies Regulation II's routing rules to its debit cards on networks it does not own (dgn-323). One firm says merchants cannot reroute these cards, and a consultancy says the second network's independence is in question (dgn-314, pulse-q05).

cards.title: Each fee line should trace to its transaction and the card's class, since the Fed found Discover charged a commercial rate it did not disclose

observed.text: From 2007 until at least 2023, Discover classified millions of consumer cards as commercial, its highest pricing tier for acquirers and merchants.
Discover did not disclose that it was charging them the commercial rate, its network had no classification controls, and Discover Bank received about 90% of the revenue gained.
The Fed put the harm to acquirers and merchants near $1 billion and now requires controls that classify and assess interchange for each of them.
Discover's public range file lists ranges only and its fuller table needs an NDA on file, while Mastercard gives eligible acquirers product-level range data on a click-through agreement.
Large UK acquirers said they must buy extra services or consultancy from the schemes to understand their fees, and many Australian payment providers reported difficulty reconciling scheme fees.
The UK requires Visa and Mastercard to give acquirers data to reconcile scheme and processing fees from July 2027. Fee logic for smaller fees is deferred to July 2029.

inference.text: The study infers that a per-transaction line naming each card's class would show an acquirer the tier it was billed, which the Fed found Discover did not disclose.
The study infers that checking the class is right also needs card range data, which Discover keeps behind an NDA.
The study infers that Capital One's plan to move meaningful credit volume onto the network raises an acquirer's stake in how the owner's cards are classified.

The study infers that fee logic for every fee line is hard for Visa and Mastercard to supply quickly, since both asked the UK regulator for more time. The deferral covers only fees earning £850,000 or less a year.

decision.question: Should each fee and interchange line trace to its transaction, merchant, card class and rule, with a flag and its correction in the same record?
options: Keep fees as cycle totals broken out by basis, as the story's portal does, and interchange as a cycle total with a variance row, as Clearway does.
Trace each line to its transaction, merchant, card class and rule, machine-readable at no cost, with flag and correction in one record and a range lookup for developers.
Do the trace and also publish a promise that the network corrects any error it finds for every affected partner, with interest, without a claim.
decision.evidence_favours: The second now, with the third put to the business and legal. The Fed found the commercial rate went undisclosed and card classification went uncontrolled (dgn-242, dgn-244). The consent order now requires classification controls for each acquirer and merchant (dgn-245). Acquirers abroad report the cost of checking fees (cross-191, cross-231). Visa and Mastercard sought more time for full fee logic in the UK (cross-229). The promise follows the RBA's remediation principle and the settlement's interest term, so its terms belong to the business (cross-232, cross-125).

position.text: The Fed found Discover charged a commercial rate it did not disclose, with no controls to classify cards. Its fuller range table needs an NDA, where Mastercard offers eligible acquirers product-level data on a click-through agreement. Visa and Mastercard told the UK regulator they could not supply fee logic for every fee within a year.

means.text: Make a statement each acquirer's finance team can reconcile the value claim, with every line tied to its transaction, the card's class and the rule that set it. Once Discover confirms its controls, say who sets each card's class and that those who assess interchange act with the independence the consent order requires. The history stays out of the story.

The portal's cycle breakdown lists assessment, authorisation and dispute fees by basis beside the cycle's transactions by merchant. It has no interchange line, though the developer settlement API returns one. Add interchange, and give each transaction its fees and card class, machine-readable at no cost. The 2027 fee notice gives old and new amounts, as Canada's Code asks, and no reason, which the RBA expects notices to carry.

In Clearway's Settlement view, the interchange variance row against the scheme file opens to its transactions, each with its card class and the rule that set it. A partner flags a line and sees the correction land in the same record. In the agent seat the flag becomes a case with an owner, as the consent order sends significant issues from acquirer and merchant complaints to the board.

The settlement API already returns interchange and assessment as line items. Add a card range lookup that returns product class and the rule behind it. Whether access needs an NDA or a click-through agreement like Mastercard's is the business's call.

objection.text: A Discover executive would say the conduct predates Capital One, the Fed fine was paid before closing and the settlement has final approval. The executive would add that building the product around it reopens the matter with prospects.

resolution.text: The product does not name the history. It shows each partner the result of classification controls the consent order already requires. The order and settlement are public, and Capital One's 2026 filings report a shareholder class action and an SEC investigation of the matter.

cards.limit: The study found no public copy of the consent order's compliance plans, which go to the Reserve Bank (cross-113, dgn-245). It found no public acquirer comment on the case, so partner need rests on UK and Australian submissions (cross-191, cross-231). The UK direction covers scheme and processing fees (cross-065), so an interchange trace would go beyond it. The study found no US rule requiring Discover to give acquirers fees they can reconcile.

cards.title: Alliances give acquirers inbound card brands and issuers' cardholders markets abroad, and the story's alliance map misdates most of them

observed.text: Discover claims 30+ network alliances with networks, issuers and payments organisations, and calls Discover Network the fastest growing by number of alliances, citing a 2025 Panoramic Research study.
Public releases date eleven of the twelve alliances on the Brightline map two to twelve years earlier than the map, from UnionPay in 2005 to Bancomat in 2022.

Of the four alliances the map rings as opened since 2024, only Egypt's fits. Egyptian Banks Company, whose site lists Meeza among its national payment schemes, announced acceptance across Egypt on 3 November 2025.
The releases say RuPay, Verve, Troy, NAPAS, mada and Uzcard run both ways, while Discover's reach page states no direction for most alliances.
Discover's reach page omits Verve, Meeza, Bancomat and Uzcard, and its cardholder map grades Nigeria and Uzbekistan with no card or ATM acceptance.
Discover's merchant page names eight alliance card brands for merchants to welcome, and its BIN page ties accepting alliance cards to loading every Discover BIN range.

inference.text: The study infers that alliances offer an acquirer inbound card brands and an issuer markets abroad for its cardholders, so one total serves neither precisely.
The study infers that an announcement date alone overstates live reach, since Discover's own map shows no acceptance in two markets whose releases announce it.

The study infers that a growth line can rest on Discover's fastest-growing claim and its five-year footnote. The study dated only the mapped alliances plus EBC, Uzcard, PayNet and AFS, so it cannot test a 'further every year' line.

decision.question: Should the story and partner surfaces present alliances as one growing total on a dated map, or by partner type and direction with each release date and live grade?
options: Keep one growing total, with the dated map and the newest alliances ringed.
Split by partner type. Acquirers see the brands their merchants can take and the BIN step. Issuers see the markets their cardholders gain, each with its release date and live grade.
Lead with Discover's fastest-growing claim and its footnote, and drop the map's years.
decision.evidence_favours: The split. Eleven of the map's twelve years and three of its four rings fail against public releases (dgn-325, dgn-328, dgn-333, dgn-336). The merchant page names eight inbound brands tied to the BIN step (dgn-187, dgn-189). Releases state direction where the reach page does not (dgn-327, dgn-192). Discover's map shows no acceptance in Uzbekistan and Nigeria, so a date alone overstates live reach (dgn-339, dgn-340). Growth can still cite Discover's fastest-growing line with its footnote (dgn-338). The business owns which alliances exist and go live. Design owns making direction, date and grade visible.

position.text: Discover claims 30+ alliances and the fastest growth by alliance count, both its own claims. American Express carries JCB in Australia, New Zealand and Canada, and Visa co-badges with the UAE's Jaywan scheme. The study found no comparative source ranking alliance breadth. Capital One's 2025 10-K ties its international network's long-term success to network licensees and meaningful global acceptance.

means.text: Replace each year on the reach map with its release date, and drop the ring and the line 'The four marked opened since 2024'. Drop 'Every connected partner reached them the same day', a timing that the BIN step also contradicts. Change the footer's 'thirty alliances with domestic networks' to 30+ alliances with networks, issuers and payments organisations.

Split alliance reach by partner type. Acquirers see the eight alliance brands Discover's merchant page names. Issuers see the markets their cardholders gain, such as Japan through JCB and India through RuPay. Carry growth with Discover's fastest-growing line and its footnote.

Each alliance shows its direction, release date and current grade on Discover's map. An acquirer's view shows whether its BIN table carries every Discover range, including the JCB and UnionPay ranges Discover's IIN summary says participants enable under their agreements.
Marcus sees each alliance's announcement beside its live grade, with markets such as Uzbekistan and Nigeria flagged where Discover's map still shows no acceptance.

objection.text: Alliances may add less than the count implies. Network Partners volume, which includes alliances along with banks and fintechs, fell from $44.5bn in 2022 to $32.8bn in 2024. Capital One's 2025 10-K gives no separate Network Partners figure.

resolution.text: Capital One's 2025 10-K says alliance participants issue cards that run on its network and support acceptance in their own markets. Showing each alliance's direction and live grade lets a partner see what applies to it without resting on the total.

cards.limit: The study found no public volume for alliances alone. Release dates mark announcements, and live acceptance can follow later (dgn-339, diners-049). Direction was not confirmed for alliances without a release found. Discover's 2024 10-K says it carries the counterparty exposure when an alliance network fails to settle. It names no party paid under that guarantee, so the card makes no claim for it (dgn-190).

cards.title: Discover's own map grades reach market by market, while its partner pages give one total and its owner names priority destinations

observed.text: Discover's partner pages give more than 185 countries and territories, and its cardholder map repeats that figure above grades showing card acceptance in 110 of 247 markets.
The map's US panel says Discover is accepted at 99% of places that take credit cards, citing Nilson, and seven partner pages checked omit it.
In July 2026 Capital One's chief executive said Discover's domestic acceptance has a few scattered gaps and international acceptance will be a long quest.
On the same call he named Mexico, the Caribbean, Canada and the UK as customers' top four destinations, where Capital One is leaning in to lift acceptance.
Discover's map puts Mexico, Canada and the UK in its top card tier, and 24 of 27 Caribbean island markets show no ATM coverage.
Discover told Travelnews it lost acceptance in Australia from 31 October 2024, and its map now grades Australia as limited for cards and ATMs.

inference.text: The study infers that the top card tier cannot show what the owner is lifting in its priority markets, so ATM grades and named acquirers matter more.
The study infers that grading adds little new exposure, since 185 and 110 already sit together on the map the partner Reach page links to.
The study infers that each grade needs an as-of date, since Discover reported losing Australian acceptance in October 2024 and its map now grades Australia limited.

decision.question: Do we state reach as Discover's headline totals, or as a dated, graded market view each partner can check against its own markets?
options: Keep the headline totals, 185 countries and one card count.
Keep one dated total and add a market view of card tier, ATM tier, named acquirers and an as-of date.
Add partner-specific views in the product, so an issuer sees its cardholders' destinations and an acquirer abroad sees arriving cards by origin market.
decision.evidence_favours: The second in the story and value proposition, with the third in Clearway and the Agent portal. Discover's map already shows 185 above grades with card acceptance in 110 markets, and the partner Reach page links to it (dgn-345, dgn-252, dgn-355). The owner names four priority destinations and frames acceptance market by market (dgn-259, dgn-356). The map's top card tier covers Mexico, Canada and the UK while most Caribbean island markets show no ATM coverage (dgn-351, dgn-352). The business owns acceptance building and what data is published. Design owns making each grade dated and checkable.

position.text: In the US, Discover's map claims acceptance at 99% of places that take credit cards. Abroad its map grades card acceptance in 110 markets, while Visa's 10-K cites more than 200 countries and territories and Mastercard's site more than 210. Stripe lets businesses in 28 countries accept Discover, against all countries for Visa and Mastercard. Capital One ties moving bigger spenders onto the network to greater international acceptance, and PaymentsJournal reported Venture X still on Visa in July 2026. In the sources checked, American Express and Mastercard state reach as totals. The study infers that Discover's per-market grade is the more checkable form.

means.text: Lead US reach with Discover's own line, 99% of places that take credit cards, with its Nilson source and date. Grade other markets for cards and ATMs, each with an as-of date and what the count includes.

Replace the reach band's flat 185 with a market view of card tier, ATM tier, named acquirers and an as-of date. Brightline is a US acquirer, so its view shows arriving cards by origin market. Replace the band's 378M with one card count, footnoted and dated, since Discover's pages give 378 million and 439 million.
An issuer sees its cardholders' top destinations against card and ATM grades, each gap named with the route behind it. It gets notice before acceptance in a market changes.
Marcus sees partners exposed to a market that rests on a single licensee, since Capital One's 10-K names interrupted licensee relationships as a threat to international acceptance.

objection.text: A graded map invites comparison of 110 markets with Visa's more than 200 and Mastercard's more than 210 countries and territories. Stripe already lists Discover for businesses in 28 countries, against all countries for Visa and Mastercard.

resolution.text: The grades are already public, beside the 185 headline, on the map the partner Reach page links to. Capital One's 10-K frames acceptance market by market. In the sources checked, American Express and Mastercard state reach as totals.

cards.limit: The study found no published thresholds for the map's tiers (dgn-353). The map grades acceptance for Discover cards, so it may not reflect every alliance brand. No page read explains the gap between 185 and 110. The study found no public data on alliance volume by direction or on network card spend abroad. The owner's plans rest on earnings calls and press reports.

cards.title: Certification is gated and planned per partner, and firm times attach mostly to the network's own steps

observed.text: Visa, Mastercard, American Express, Discover and UnionPay, the networks whose path this study could read, each put a signed contract or reviewed request before certification.
US rules require a credit card system operator to take risk-based steps before it authorises an issuer or acquirer.
A 2023 U.S. Payments Forum paper says Discover, Mastercard and Visa draw certification cases from each partner's configuration or session, and UnionPay's onboarding guide says the same.

The same paper says Visa, Mastercard, American Express and Discover each run a programme for acquirers to test terminals themselves, and Mastercard's Fast Track reuses approvals for identical terminals.
Mastercard's Mastercom and Mastercard Send checklists call their timings service levels and name an escalation route, and American Express and PULSE publish turnarounds for certificates and user IDs.
Visa and Mastercard Send give hedged ranges for the whole journey, and Mastercard tells Send partners not to plan their project on its figures.

inference.text: The study reads the US rule as not reaching debit-only networks or sandbox access, since it turns on the operator's own credit card and on authorising issuers and acquirers.
The study infers that Rich's rule is stricter than peer practice, since Visa says timing is the first question on nearly every client's mind.

decision.question: Do the network's commitments on its own steps count as timings under 'No timings anywhere in the product', and what replaces the durations removed?
options: Remove every timing, network commitments included, and show owners and passed dates only
Remove durations set by the partner's pace, internal estimates and journey ranges, and keep a network commitment only where the business will stand behind it with an escalation route
Publish hedged ranges for the whole journey, as Visa and Mastercard Send do
decision.evidence_favours: Until Rich rules, every timing stays off every surface. For his ruling, the evidence favours the second. Mastercard and American Express publish commitments on their own steps, and Mastercard gives its service levels an escalation route (mastercard-078, amex-385, mastercard-418). Mastercard tells Send partners not to plan on journey ranges (mastercard-081). Visa says timing is nearly every client's first question (visa-427). A booked certification window is a network commitment, so the ruling covers it too.

position.text: Discover is level on the gate, on cases drawn from each acquirer's request form and on terminal self-certification since 2013. Outside PULSE's credential promise, this study found no Discover turnaround for its own steps, while Mastercard and American Express publish them.

means.text: Retire 'The sandbox credentials, promoted' in the credentials table and go-live checklist, and 'Production uses your existing credentials' in the developer steps. Visa, Mastercard and American Express issue production credentials separately. Remove every duration and the week axis from the roadmap chart, along with the agent's 'Week N of 9' and the pre-signature 'Nine weeks from signature'. Move the leftover 'Run the suite' copy to the observed model adopted on 7 September 2026.

Its 78-day median to live, nine-day risk review, twelve and eight working days, six to nine weeks and eleven weeks to live break the no-timings rule. Show the owner on each step instead, as Mastercard Send names who assists each phase. Move 'Run the suite' and 'Run all 61' to the story's observed model.

The certification guide already derives cases from configuration, which is parity with Discover, Mastercard, Visa and UnionPay. Replace 'Typically 20 to 30' and '21 cases for a typical acquirer' with one worked example, since cases vary by partner. Remove the eight-day median and the quickstart's 'Ten minutes'. Retire 'The same credentials, promoted' in the environments table and docs index.

Keep certification process off the marketing view. The developer site states that cases follow each partner's configuration and acquirers can test terminals themselves, as parity with peers. It keeps stating that certification needs a participation agreement, as Rich chose on scope 1.

objection.text: Visa and Mastercard Send publish hedged journey ranges, and Visa says timing is the first question on nearly every client's mind. Removing every timing would leave partners without an answer those peers give.

resolution.text: The objection narrows the rule without overturning it. Mastercard tells Send partners not to plan on its ranges, while it and American Express stand behind commitments on their own steps. The study recommends keeping such commitments, subject to Rich's ruling, and leaving journey ranges out.

cards.limit: The certification sentences rest on a 2023 trade-body paper, and membership portals for issuers and acquirers were not seen. Discover's stage order rests on a portal bundle not re-read on 25 September 2026 (dgn-172). This study found no readable production path for the US PIN debit networks or JCB (pulse-002, nyce-019, culiance-013, shazam-013, jcb-016). A published figure says nothing about how often the network meets it.

cards.title: Discover's public pages count cards and total spend for merchants and give no figure for what network cardholders spend with them

observed.text: Discover's acceptance page cites over 378 million cards and 622 billion dollars of 2024 spend, and its home page over 439 million and 634 billion for 2025.
The card count includes network alliance cards while the spend covers Discover, Diners Club and PULSE, so dividing one by the other gives no spend per card.
None of the pages in the 61-entry public sitemap gives spend per card, ticket size or sales delivered, and the acceptance page promises incremental sales without a figure.
Stripe told merchants on cost-plus pricing that migrated Capital One debit cards would likely carry higher interchange than they did on Mastercard.
Capital One's chief executive said merchants ask how much volume a network brings, and that Capital One likes to show merchants data on the value it adds.
Capital One Offers is linked to eligible Capital One credit card accounts, and PULSE's Discover Debit page lists no merchant offers for community issuers.

inference.text: The study infers that a card count does not answer a merchant facing higher interchange, since it says nothing about the sales those cards bring.
The study infers that a per-merchant sales figure fits the owner's stated aim of showing merchants data on the value it adds.
The study infers that a network offers layer would give credit unions and fintechs offers they did not build, as Visa's community issuer programme does.

decision.question: Should the acquirer's merchant view and the marketing pages argue merchant value from what network cardholders spend at each merchant, beside card counts?
options: Keep the reach argument of card count, total spend and countries, with one dated figure set
Add a per-merchant figure of sales from network cards in the acquirer's merchant view and on the marketing page
Add the per-merchant figure and a network offers layer open to partner issuers, kept apart from Capital One Offers
decision.evidence_favours: The second option. Design owns the view, and the business owns releasing merchant-level sales data under data-use terms such as those proposed for partner facts. The public pages give no per-card or per-merchant figure (dgn-357), American Express argues from spend per card (amex-448), and the owner says merchants ask about volume (dgn-359). The offers layer in the third option is a business decision for Discover leadership (visa-090, amex-288, dgn-237).

position.text: American Express argues from spend per card and gives acquirers card-linked offers and targeting models. Visa runs a merchant offers programme for community issuers, and Mastercard sells loyalty services to issuers and merchants. NYCE's owner FIS pairs an offers network with NYCE routing. Discover's DCX page names no partners and keeps its September 2021 attribution copy.

means.text: Give acquirers and merchants a reason to welcome the card beyond reach, led by what network cardholders spend. Date each figure and name its source.

The marketing page's sizer and the panel 2 deal can show invented network-cardholder spend in Brightline's merchant categories. The reach band should date its 378 million figure and name its source. Brightline's partner portal Merchants view can show network-card sales per merchant once live.

The agent sees which partners have offers switched on. A live issuer such as Meridian Trust would switch offers on as a new module. Plain terms on who sees cardholder data sit beside it, marked as a proposal for the business.

objection.text: A Discover executive could object that Capital One Offers already covers thousands of retailers, and its chief executive says Capital One is well along in direct merchant-funded deals. A network offers layer would duplicate that and pass smaller issuers deals the owner negotiated.

resolution.text: The per-merchant figure needs no offers layer, so the design step stands apart from that choice. An offers layer need not carry the owner's deals. In 2024 American Express moved its Amex Offers team into its US consumer business, and its network site still offers partner issuers a card-linked offers platform.

cards.limit: Discover's gated portals may hold merchant reporting that the public pages omit (dgn-231). American Express gives 60% on its acceptance page and 58% on its offers page, each its own comparison with non-card members (amex-447, amex-324). The higher-interchange view comes from Stripe and a merchant consultancy (dgn-215, dgn-213). This study found no source showing a merchant can reconcile a network sales figure with its own statement.

cards.title: Four of six issuing platforms checked document no Discover issuing, and Discover's fintech page names no provider that carries it

observed.text: Stripe Issuing supports Mastercard and Visa and has a business pick one at onboarding, and Adyen Issuing creates cards on the same two.
Highnote's issuing guides name Visa and Mastercard and name Discover only for acquiring, and Lithic's transaction schema lists American Express, Visa, Mastercard, Maestro and Interlink.
SoFi Tech Solutions is integrated with Discover and PULSE, and says a programme's primary network is usually Mastercard or Visa.
Marqeta says its platform is certified on Discover's April 2026 release, and tells clients the Discover changes alter nothing in how they use the platform.
Discover's fintech page names Wellthi, Finexio and Mystifly and no processor, sponsor bank or programme manager, and its Partner Directory holds 37 tap-on-mobile and six stored-token products.
Discover's US Find an Acquirer list of 43 names omits Adyen, whose public price list includes Discover acceptance.

inference.text: The study infers a fintech or programme manager meets a network inside its issuing platform's set-up, since Stripe and SoFi Tech Solutions place the network choice there.
The study infers part of the gap is visibility. Marqeta and SoFi Tech Solutions carry Discover, yet Discover's fintech page and Partner Directory name neither, and its US acquirer list omits Adyen.

decision.question: Should the fintech and programme manager experience start from platforms that already carry Discover, with a public list, or wait until the business commits to courting fintech issuers?
options: Add a provider-first path, with a public list of platforms carrying Discover by product and country and a fintech story variant that starts inside one of them
Keep the direct join journey as the only path, as the Brightline story shows for an acquirer
Hold every fintech surface until the business decides whether to court fintech issuers
decision.evidence_favours: The provider-first path. Stripe and SoFi Tech Solutions put the network choice inside their own set-up, Marqeta is certified on Discover's current release, and Discover's own pages name no issuing provider (dgn-265, dgn-269, dgn-363, dgn-365). Which platforms to court, and Adyen's blended Discover pricing, stay with the business.

position.text: Discover is behind Visa and Mastercard on the issuing platforms checked. Stripe, Adyen, Highnote and Lithic document both, and none of the four documents Discover issuing. American Express admitted Marqeta and Lithic to its Agile Partnership Platform in 2025. On Stripe, Discover acceptance covers 28 countries, against all countries for Visa and Mastercard. Adyen prices Discover at a blended 3.95% and PULSE at interchange plus 0.60%, as it prices Visa.

means.text: Name the processors, sponsor banks and programme managers that carry Discover, and what each carries, since Discover's fintech page names none today. Where a processor states it is certified on the current release, present that work as done for its clients, as Marqeta states.

Publish a list of platforms that carry Discover, by country, showing credit, debit, PULSE, Diners Club, disputes and tokens for each. Discover's Partner Directory today holds only tap-on-mobile and stored-token products, so this needs its own category or page.

A participant record carries facts inherited from its processor, such as the certified release, with the processor named as the source. A processor field should then remove the steps that processor has already covered.
A fintech variant would begin inside an issuing platform that already carries Discover, such as Marqeta or SoFi Tech Solutions, with Discover switched on there.

objection.text: A counter-argument is that the owner now has its own business card platform, having paid about 4.5 billion dollars for Brex. On that view, small fintech issuers may bring too little volume to justify courting Stripe's and Adyen's issuing platforms.

resolution.text: Which fintechs to court stays a business choice. More than five months after the 7 April close, Brex's site names Mastercard and Visa licences, so ownership alone has not moved its issuing. Network Partners volume rose in 2022 and fell in 2023 and 2024, and Discover's filing warns weaker merchant acceptance could hurt its ability to keep Network Partners. A list of where Discover is already carried draws on public facts, such as Marqeta's certification and Moorwand's UK Diners Club licence.

cards.limit: Discover issuing at i2c, Fiserv, FIS and TSYS was not confirmed. Highnote's and Lithic's omissions are weaker evidence than Stripe's and Adyen's plain statements. Thredd said in 2024 that its Discover work would begin with Diners Club virtual cards, and its live status was not checked (diners-056). Adyen's blended Discover rate may include interchange, so it is not shown to be a premium. Network Partners volume mixes alliances, fintechs and Discover's commercial payments network, so its fall cannot be tied to fintech issuing (dgn-369). Checkout.com, Braintree and PayPal were not checked for issuing.

cards.title: Where money can land is part of reach, and Capital One warned its own debit customers that some instant transfers may stop

observed.text: Capital One warns its debit customers that some payroll providers, including Branch Messenger and PayActiv, may not support instant transfers to the new cards.
It attributes the change to the network the cards run on, and says some merchants, such as Cash App, still allow instant transfers.
Venmo's help page added participating Discover debit cards between archive copies of 23 February and 18 April 2026, and TabaPay says its push-to-card payouts run over Discover.
Richmond Fed researchers say Visa Direct and Mastercard Send reach nearly all US debit cards, and Visa reports more than 650 Visa Direct partners in fiscal 2025.
A June 2026 payouts guide from Routable names Visa Direct and Mastercard Send and does not mention Discover.
Neither the Discover Deliver page nor PULSE's articles give an originator count, and the Developer Center's Funds Transfer heading lists no public API.

inference.text: The study infers that push reach depends on issuer participation as well as originators, since Venmo limits eligibility to cards that participate in instant transfer services.
The study infers that some pushes to PULSE-routed cards may run on a rival's service, since Mastercard Send's public sandbox lists PULSE test cards.
The study infers that an issuer weighing Discover Debit would check whether its cardholders can still receive instant pay, given Capital One's warning to its own customers.

decision.question: Do we count who can pay out to our cards as part of the network's reach, shown to issuers and developers, or leave push payments to a product page?
options: Leave Discover Deliver as a product page, as Discover does today.
Show issuers which originators pay out to their cards and which do not yet, and give developers a Deliver reference and sandbox.
Lead the value proposition with a push-reach figure beside acceptance.
decision.evidence_favours: The second. Capital One warned its own debit customers that some payroll providers may not support instant transfers, and attributed this to the network (dgn-299, dgn-300, dgn-301). Coverage exists and is uncounted, since Venmo, Cash App and TabaPay pay out to Discover debit (cross-216, dgn-371, dgn-303). A payouts guide omits Discover, and the Developer Center lists no public funds-transfer API (cross-217, dgn-169). The third option needs an originator count, and the study found none in public. The business owns originator enablement. Design owns making coverage visible per issuer and giving developers a reference.

position.text: Richmond Fed researchers credit Visa Direct and Mastercard Send with near-universal US debit reach, and Visa reports more than 650 Visa Direct partners. The study found no Discover originator count, and a June 2026 payouts guide omits Discover. The study found no American Express push-to-card evidence, so that comparison is unknown. Visa has launched stablecoin settlement for US issuers and acquirers, and Mastercard has bought a stablecoin infrastructure firm. The study found no Discover network position on stablecoins, though Capital One's 10-K lists them among payment forms it competes with. Capital One is among 21 institutions that announced a stablecoin company plan on 1 September 2026.

means.text: Count push reach beside acceptance and alliances, as the originators that pay out to Discover and PULSE cards and the issuers that receive. For issuers, cite PULSE's point that institutions receive interchange on every debit-network account-to-account transaction.

Present Discover Deliver as a product with its own reference and sandbox, under the Funds Transfer heading that currently lists no public API. State which card ranges can receive a payout, and give no payout duration.
An issuer sees which originators pay out to its cards and which do not yet, starting with the payroll providers Capital One names, with its own participation shown.
Originator coverage is tracked as a network measure, with each gap named and the issuer partners it touches.

objection.text: Venmo, Cash App and TabaPay already pay out to Discover debit cards, so the gap may close without a counted measure. Capital One's warning may also be a migration artefact.

resolution.text: Capital One's warning appears in an August 2025 archive copy and on the live page in September 2026. PULSE says debit networks carry an estimated 5 billion US money-movement transactions a year, and names earned-wage access and gig payouts among the transfers they carry. The study found no public count of originators that reach Discover or PULSE cards.

cards.limit: The study found no count of originators that push to Discover or PULSE cards. Current eligibility at Branch, PayActiv and PayPal was not checked. Venmo's change is dated only from archive copies. Live push coverage for PULSE cards through Mastercard Send was not confirmed. Stablecoin settlement is a business lever and stays out of this card's recommendations.

cards.title: Discover's US acquirer rates are confidential, so the deal should show each acquirer its standard rate and any incentive on separate lines

observed.text: Discover's US acquirer interchange chart is confidential and sits behind a code the acquirer issues, and its merchant acceptance page states no price.
Canada's Code requires networks to publish standard interchange, wholesale discount and acquirer assessment rates, and Discover and American Express publish theirs there.
In the United States, Visa and Mastercard publish interchange and leave merchant pricing to acquirers.
Adyen prices Mastercard at interchange plus 0.60% and Discover at a blended 3.95%, each plus 13 cents, and Stripe's standard price is one blended rate for domestic cards.
If approved after its November hearing, the Visa and Mastercard settlement would let merchants ask cardholders for lower-cost cards and surcharge Visa credit whether or not they surcharge Discover.
Discover's 2024 10-K says it competes on customised services and pricing that includes incentives and rebates, and it discloses no amounts.

inference.text: The study infers that how an acquirer prices Discover decides whether a merchant can see Discover's cost at all, and so whether the settlement's preference clause could favour it.
The study infers that publishing a US standard schedule would bring parity with Visa and Mastercard on interchange, and no source shows it would win acquirer volume.
The study infers that a view of its own margin could move an acquirer to present Discover, since the acquirer sets the merchant's price. No source confirms it.

decision.question: Should the deal and portal show each acquirer its standard rate, any incentive and its margin now, or wait for the business to decide on a published US schedule?
options: Keep selling reach and incremental sales with no price, as Discover's acceptance page does now.
Show each acquirer its standard rate and any incentive on separate lines, with a margin view built from its own merchant pricing.
The business publishes a US standard schedule, as Discover already does in Canada, and design builds the same views on it.
decision.evidence_favours: The second now, with the third put to the business. Discover competes on incentives and rebates, so separate lines show an acquirer which part was negotiated (dgn-071). Publication would bring parity with Visa and Mastercard on interchange (visa-238, mastercard-090). No source shows it would win acquirer volume, and Capital One's deal case assumed existing network pricing (dgn-221).

position.text: Discover's US acquirer chart is confidential, where Visa and Mastercard publish US interchange. In Canada Discover publishes its schedule as the Code requires, as American Express does. Adyen passes Mastercard through at interchange plus 0.60% and prices Discover at a blended 3.95%. Capital One says more surcharging could cut card use, and the pending settlement would let merchants surcharge Visa whatever they do on Discover.

means.text: Until the business decides on a US schedule, the value claim is the acquirer's own economics on network volume. Show the standard rate and any incentive or rebate on separate lines, so the acquirer sees which part was negotiated.

The public sizer can add the reader's margin on network volume from the reader's own inputs. It can show blended-rate and interchange-plus merchants apart, and keep Brightline Bank's numbers off the page. The deal the network sends Dana lists a standard schedule and no incentive, so any incentive offered gets its own line.
Settlement can show the acquirer's margin on network volume from merchant pricing the acquirer enters, since the acquirer sets the merchant's price. It shows no other brand's figures.

objection.text: A Discover executive would say Capital One's deal case assumed existing network pricing on the volume it moves. The executive would add that a published rate hands rivals a target and invites merchants to demand the lowest figure. Since the cardholder picks the credit card at the till, the executive would expect a cheaper acquirer rate to bring little volume.

resolution.text: The recommended views publish nothing and work at any price level, so they leave the deal case intact. If approved, the settlement would let a merchant ask for a lower-cost card, and the cardholder would still choose. The study infers price needs a companion reason for an acquirer to present Discover.

cards.limit: Discover's US rates, incentives and acquirer margins are not public (dgn-064, dgn-071), and the study found no public source comparing acquirer margin by network. No source gives Adyen's reason for pricing Discover apart. The settlement awaits final approval, and the court rejected the 2024 version (mastercard-413, cross-094). The settlement terms here were read in Visa's section only.

cards.title: Covered banks earn capped interchange on Discover debit as on Visa and Mastercard, so the issuer case should split by asset size

observed.text: Regulation II does not apply where the network processor is also the issuer. Capital One's 10-K says its bank earns an issuer rate instead of interchange on cards issued on its own network.
In 2024 covered transactions on Discover averaged 23 cents on a 32.56 dollar ticket, close to the cap, at a share the Fed rounds to zero.
Covered issuers may not receive more from a network in a year than they pay it, and in 2023 they received 0.65 billion dollars against 0.99 billion paid.
Below 10 billion dollars in assets the cap and net compensation rule fall away and the network sets the rate, though the two-network routing rule still applies.
Chime drew 55% of its 2024 revenue from debit interchange and says it depends on its partner banks keeping the small issuer exemption.
Visa publishes its exempt debit rates, while PULSE sells Discover Debit to community banks and credit unions on an all-in programme fee through a lead form.

inference.text: The study infers that a covered bank's case on Discover rests on measured results and net network cost. The cap and net compensation rule bind it as on Visa and Mastercard.
The study infers that exempt banks and the programme managers they sponsor are where Discover Debit's rate can differ from rivals, because below the threshold the network sets it.
The study infers that published rates would help exempt issuers compare networks, since the Fed publishes network averages so small issuers can compare revenue.

decision.question: Should the network publish Discover Debit's exempt issuer rates, so a community bank or programme manager can model yield on its own mix?
options: Keep the all-in programme fee and the lead form, with yield shown inside a sales analysis.
Show modelled yield after routing inside the deal builder only.
Publish exempt rates with a public calculator of yield after routing on the partner's own mix.
decision.evidence_favours: Publishing, on the benchmark and as the study's inference. Visa publishes its exempt debit rates, and PULSE sells Discover Debit through a lead form and publishes no interchange schedule (visa-445, pulse-034, pulse-011). The Fed publishes network averages so small issuers can compare revenue (cross-240). No source measures how issuers respond to published rates. Whether third-party issuers receive the adviser-quoted rates is not public (dgn-222). The business owns the rates, and design owns the asset-size split and the calculator.

position.text: For covered banks Discover is at parity, since the cap binds on it as on Visa and Mastercard. On rate legibility it is behind, because Visa publishes exempt rates and PULSE publishes no interchange schedule. Exempt yield for third-party issuers is not public, and PULSE cites one bank whose Discover Debit contribution rose 45%.

means.text: Split the issuer debit case by asset size. For covered banks, lead with results measured on the bank's own volume and a net network bill inside the net compensation line. For exempt banks and programme managers, lead with interchange on the partner's own mix and one programme fee.

Northgate's issuer set-up asks for asset size first. Above 10 billion dollars it shows interchange at the cap and net network cost. Below it, it models interchange after routing on Northgate's ticket size and card-present share.
If the network publishes exempt rates, show them in a readable calculator a community bank or programme manager can use without an account. Keep Visa figures off the page.
The deal builder carries the asset-size input. It flags a covered-bank offer whose payments and incentives, signing bonuses included, would exceed that bank's fees to the network.

objection.text: A community bank would note that merger commenters told the OCC Discover debit fees were higher than capped debit. An analyst expects merchants to push back on higher debit interchange paid to a big bank that buys a network. A Discover Debit card's second network must sit outside Capital One, which owns PULSE, and merchants may route to it where the card and channel allow.

resolution.text: The objection sets the design, so the calculator shows yield after routing on the partner's own PIN and card-not-present shares. Single-message networks carried 6.6% of card-not-present debit transactions in 2023. The study infers that front-of-card pricing mostly holds online. Merchants ultimately pay interchange to issuers, so the value set should say which product serves which partner. Position Discover Debit for exempt issuers, and PULSE for merchants against Visa and Mastercard dual-message debit.

cards.limit: The Discover debit rates the study found are adviser quotes for Capital One's migrated cards, and whether third-party exempt issuers receive them is not public (dgn-222, dgn-212, pulse-011). The Fed's 2024 Discover average mostly reflects Discover's own three-party cards (cross-109, dgn-077). A North Dakota court vacated Regulation II in August 2025 and stayed its order pending appeal, and a Kentucky court upheld it (cross-244, cross-097). The cap remains in effect while the litigation continues (cross-097). The Fed's 2023 proposal to lower the cap was unfinalised in Capital One's February 2026 10-K (dgn-079).

cards.title: Visa's monitoring and Mastercard's rules credit disputes resolved early, while the study found no public Discover dispute line or rule on early resolution

observed.text: Visa's monitoring ratio for acquirers and merchants leaves out disputes resolved through pre-dispute tools, when they resolve before Visa's data extract.
Mastercard's rules say an issuer need not raise a chargeback once the cardholder is reimbursed through Mastercom Collaboration, Ethoca or an equivalent procedure.

American Express says under 0.030% of US transactions became disputes reaching merchants in 2025, and that Substitute Receipts helped resolve over 80% of unrecognised-charge disputes without the merchant.
The study found no public Discover dispute rules or monitoring programme, and two chargeback vendors cite about 1% and 100 chargebacks a month as its line.
Discover markets Fraud Alerts to US businesses to help prevent chargebacks, and its Standard tier is free.
A dispute-analytics vendor says merchants pay per chargeback alert whatever the outcome, and another vendor says Ethoca and CDRN each reach Discover through one reason code.

inference.text: In the study's inference, Visa's monitoring and Mastercard's rules give partners a counted reason to settle disputes early, and Discover's public material states none.
In the study's inference, free Fraud Alerts Standard can anchor early resolution, though whether a refund after an alert keeps a dispute out of any count is unknown.
In the study's inference, where Capital One issued the card, the network's owner holds the data to review a claim first and has money at stake in the outcome.

decision.question: Should the network publish its dispute monitoring line and state that a dispute resolved early, including after a Fraud Alert, does not count against merchants or acquirers?
options: Publish the line, the evidence standard, any fee and how early resolution counts, and show prevented disputes in partner views
Publish outcomes only, such as the share of disputes settled before reaching merchants, without a line
Keep case-by-case handling and market Fraud Alerts as today
decision.evidence_favours: The first. Visa publishes its lines, and Visa and Mastercard credit early resolution in monitoring or rules (visa-338, visa-337, mastercard-215). American Express publishes a dispute outcome (amex-282). Discover's line surfaces only through vendors (dgn-288, dgn-376). The study has no evidence on whether acquirers prefer case-by-case handling.

position.text: Visa publishes its monitoring lines, Visa and Mastercard credit early resolution, and American Express publishes a dispute outcome. The study found no Discover line, rules or outcome in public, and a vendor says Discover decides consequences case by case. Discover does offer free Fraud Alerts Standard, while rival alert services charge per alert.

means.text: State that a dispute resolved before chargeback does not count against the merchant or the acquirer, and publish the share settled before reaching merchants. Build early resolution on the free Fraud Alerts Standard with no per-alert fee. The line, the evidence standard and any fee belong in the partner rules, with a warning before any fee applies.

Panel 9's activity can include a dispute on a Capital One card that the network settled before chargeback, with the evidence used. Brightline Bank's Disputes page can show each merchant's disputes as prevented, open or charged back against the published line. The deal's per-dispute fee should say whether it covers disputes settled early.
The Disputes view tracks open cases by stage today. It can add a prevented state beside open and charged-back cases, with the evidence used for each.
Marcus sees which acquirers and payment facilitators are nearing the published line before any consequence applies.

objection.text: A merchant could cite American Express's merchant FAQ, which asks why it seems to always side with the customer in a dispute. The Federal Reserve found Discover improperly classified millions of credit cards as commercial for interchange, and that Discover Bank received about 90% of the revenue gained. The study infers that an owner that issues the card and settles disputes upstream has its own bank's money at stake.

resolution.text: The evidence standard and each upstream result should be visible to the merchant, and a prevented dispute should count in the merchant's favour. The same rules should apply to Capital One cards and partner issuers' cards. Capital One told the OCC it would invest in the network's payment and fraud dispute resolution processes.

cards.limit: The Discover picture rests on public pages and on chargeback-service firms' guides, one of them an authorised Ethoca and Verifi reseller (dgn-288, dgn-376, dgn-291). The gated Disputes Portal may hold thresholds and tools the study could not see (dgn-122). The American Express figures are its own (amex-282). In the study's inference, any upstream settlement covers only cards Capital One issues (dgn-047, dgn-055). The study has no evidence on whether acquirers would prefer a published line.

cards.title: Single-message networks carried little online debit in 2023, which DOJ alleges Visa's cliff pricing and tokens held down, and PULSE markets a routable token

observed.text: Merchants have had the right to direct debit routing since October 2011, and card-not-present debit came under the two-network rule on 1 July 2023.
The Fed says single-message networks were still used relatively rarely online in 2023, carrying 6.6% of card-not-present debit transactions, up from 6.1% in 2021.
DOJ's September 2024 complaint alleges Visa uses cliff pricing and holds de facto exclusive routing deals with over 180 of its largest merchants and acquirers.
It also alleges tokenised card-not-present debit may be effectively non-contestable, and that a tiny fraction of it reached an unaffiliated network in 2023.
A processor notice says Visa and Interlink charge merchants 0.015%, minimum one cent, on approved card-not-present token authorisations from June 2026.

PULSE says its Side-by-Side Token Service routes tokenised card-on-file debit over PULSE and other enabled unaffiliated networks, and enrolment is by contact form with no published specification or fee.

inference.text: The study infers that a transaction routed over PULSE would not carry Visa's or Interlink's new token authorisation fee, which applies to their own token authorisations.
The study infers that price alone does not make PULSE's case against STAR, Accel or Maestro, which averaged below it in 2024.
The study infers that incentive terms an acquirer can read before signing would set PULSE apart from the cliff pricing DOJ alleges, if its own terms carry no cliffs.

decision.question: Should PULSE publish routing incentive terms without cliffs and a Side-by-Side token specification and fee?
options: Keep bilateral fixed-term incentive deals and token enrolment by contact form.
Publish the token specification and fee only.
Publish incentive terms without cliffs, the token specification and fee, and give acquirers a routing view on their own data.
decision.evidence_favours: The third, as the study's inference. PULSE's 2024 average interchange sat above STAR, Accel and Maestro (dgn-076, star-005, accel-004, cross-146). DOJ alleges cliff pricing and tokens hold routing down (cross-032, visa-447, visa-463). Visa and Interlink now charge merchants per card-not-present token authorisation, while PULSE's token enrolment is a contact form (visa-414, interlink-001, pulse-005). Capital One lists merchant and acquirer routing strategies as a risk to PULSE volume (pulse-023). Whether Discover's own incentive terms carry cliffs is not public, so the term must be adopted before it can be claimed (dgn-070). The business owns terms and fees, and design owns the routing view and the specification page.

position.text: On 2024 averages PULSE's interchange sat below Visa and Mastercard dual-message debit and above STAR, Accel and Maestro. It markets a routable card-on-file token, and NYCE, STAR and Accel also list tokenised debit. The study found no public figure for its routed share or token use.

means.text: If the network adopts incentives without cliffs, write them as a contract term an acquirer can read before signing. Offer approval and fraud results by route on the acquirer's own traffic in place of a promised rate.

If the network adopts terms without cliffs, show deal incentives as a per-transaction rate that does not reprice past a volume line. Keep 'your own least-cost table' as the partner's rule, with no promise that PULSE heads it.
Give Bayline a routing view with eligible debit volume, the share routed to PULSE, and approvals and fraud by route. A token in the record shows the networks it can route to.
Give the Side-by-Side Token Service its own page with a readable specification and fee, where PULSE today offers a contact form.

objection.text: An acquirer would say Discover's 10-K for 2024 said Visa's arrangements with some merchants and acquirers discourage routing to PULSE. The same filing says Discover made fixed-term incentive arrangements of its own. On 2024 average interchange PULSE also sat above STAR and Accel. A no-cliff promise from a network that discloses no terms is another sales line.

resolution.text: The objection is fair, so any no-cliff promise has to be a published term. Against STAR, Accel and Maestro the case rests on approvals measured on the acquirer's own traffic. STAR and Accel also list tokenised debit, so the token sets PULSE apart from Visa and Interlink only. Single-message fraud figures do not separate PULSE from STAR, since both are single-message networks.

cards.limit: DOJ's cliff, exclusivity and token claims are allegations, and motions are due in August 2027 (cross-049). The court denied Visa's motion to dismiss in June 2025 (cross-137). The study found no public figure for PULSE's routed share since July 2023 or for use of its token service. Capital One does not break out PULSE volume (pulse-022, pulse-005). The token fee notice comes from Fiserv, which runs STAR and Accel (visa-414, star-010, accel-009). Whether Discover's own incentive terms carry cliffs is not public (dgn-070).

cards.title: Visa and Mastercard fold services into rising fees, while Discover calls four services free and sends partners fewer changes, and states neither as a promise

observed.text: Visa's value-added services revenue grew 24% in fiscal 2025, against 11% growth in its net revenue.
Visa's rules make every US issuer pay Visa Advanced Authorization fees, whether or not it uses the data.
In April 2026 Visa and Mastercard each added services, token services among them, to a US bundle fee and raised its rate.
Several UK acquirers told their regulator they had bought some Mastercard or Visa services by accident, and acquirers said they could not identify the merchants triggering behavioural fees.
Discover says Enhanced Decisioning and Fraud Alerts Standard cost nothing to use, and PULSE says DebitProtect is included for all participants and Discover Debit benefits cost issuers nothing.

Marqeta's 2026 log files 18 of its 58 Visa and Mastercard items as Marqeta changes to support the release. All three Discover and PULSE items sit under headings of no impact on client card programmes.

inference.text: In the study's inference, Discover's four no-cost services stand in contrast to Visa and Mastercard, which charge for risk and token services through mandatory or bundled fees.
In the study's inference, fewer Discover changes mean less processor and acquirer work each release, though the counts reflect only what each platform chose to list.
In the study's inference, the UK findings show unclear scheme service charges adding acquirer work, which a named inclusion promise could reduce for Discover partners.

decision.question: Should Discover and PULSE state one public promise that named services come with the network at no separate charge, starting with the four their pages already call free?
options: Promise inclusion for the four services with public no-cost statements, each named beside the partner type it serves
Promise those four and add tokens and account updating once Discover's pricing for them is confirmed
Keep services free or priced case by case, with no stated promise
decision.evidence_favours: The first. Four services already carry public no-cost statements (dgn-294, dgn-295, pulse-032, pulse-075), while Visa and Mastercard raised bundle fees that include token services (visa-465, mastercard-421). The study found no Discover pricing for tokens or account updating. No source tests whether partners weigh such a promise when they choose a network.

position.text: Discover and PULSE publish no-cost statements for four services, and American Express also calls its Enhanced Authorization risk-data service free. Fiserv's spring 2026 merchant notice lists four Discover changes against 16 from Visa and 12 from Mastercard. SoFi says no 2025 or 2026 Discover, PULSE or STAR mandate affected it or its clients. The study found no Discover page presenting these services together as one promise.

means.text: State one promise across Discover and PULSE that named services come with the network at no separate charge. Name each service beside the partner type it serves, such as Enhanced Decisioning for merchants and acquirers and DebitProtect for PULSE participants. Premium tiers such as Fraud Alerts Premium stay priced.

The catalogue already marks Contactless as Included. Its Decisioning is a network score priced at 0.5 basis points, while Discover's Enhanced Decisioning routes merchant data to issuers at no cost to participate. The business should say which one Brightline Bank gets, and mark it Included if it is the no-cost service. The monthly statement can then list included services at no charge beside each fee line.
Clearway has no products view today. The live participant overview can list each included service for its partner type as on or not yet switched on, since some need certification first.
Marcus sees which included services each partner has not switched on. This extends the Decisioning not adopted note already on his review agenda.

objection.text: Visa's value-added services revenue grew 24% in fiscal 2025, and in November 2024 Mastercard targeted high-teens yearly growth in its services line to 2027. A Discover executive could argue that promising inclusion forgoes that kind of growth. Capital One's 10-K warns it may be unable to offer network partners adequate pricing while keeping sufficient net revenue. Stripe told cost-plus merchants that Capital One debit cards moved onto Discover would likely carry higher interchange than on Mastercard.

resolution.text: The promise names only services Discover's pages already describe as free or no cost, so it gives up no fee those pages show, and premium tiers stay priced. Discover's own fee changes, debit included, should be priced on each partner's volume before they land. Australia's regulator expects fee notices to state expected outcomes for participants. The UK regulator now requires Visa and Mastercard to give acquirers fee data they can reconcile.

cards.limit: Discover treats its US acquirer fee chart as confidential, so a no-cost statement on a product page may not match an invoice (dgn-064). The study found no Discover pricing for tokens or account updating. Change counts come from one issuer processor's log and one acquirer's notice, and reflect only what each lists (dgn-296, cross-248). PayPal's two 2026 guides name Discover among networks that change rules yet list only Visa and Mastercard items (cross-249). Discover's announcements sit behind EASI registration and PULSE bulletins are not public, so the study may miss changes (dgn-164, pulse-017).

cards.title: Discover's owner competes with the banks and credit unions the network serves, and neither merger approval's published text records a condition on how the network treats them

observed.text: Capital One has owned Discover's networks since 18 May 2025, and it was the largest US credit card issuer by outstanding balances at the end of 2025.
Its 10-K says its banking businesses compete with banks, savings and loan associations and credit unions for loans and deposits.
Neither the Fed order nor the OCC letter records a condition on how the networks treat other issuers or their data.
The fee assurance on record is a stated intent, given to the OCC and the Fed, to raise no network fees as a result of the merger.
PULSE and Network Partners carried 58% of Discover's 2024 network volume, and Capital One valued its network and financial partner relationships at 1.5 billion dollars.
Capital One's 10-K says it will use its new networks, customer base and data to drive value for merchants, consumers and small businesses.

inference.text: The study infers that, for an issuer, the prototypes' record would describe its programme to a network whose owner competes with it for loans and deposits.
The study infers that written, checkable terms would help protect the partner relationships Capital One valued at 1.5 billion dollars, a value it based partly on estimated attrition.

decision.question: Should the partner experience make the network's separation from its owner's issuing business checkable, by showing who reads each partner fact?
options: Leave ownership unaddressed, as PULSE's About page does today
Show who can read each partner fact and a partner-visible log of network-side views, with no written terms yet
Add plain data-use and fair-treatment terms beside the access log, marked as proposals for the business to approve
decision.evidence_favours: The second option now, with the third drafted for the business. Neither approval records a condition on partner treatment or data (cross-177, cross-178, cross-116), and the fee assurance is a stated intent (cross-179). PULSE's About page still calls it independent and does not name Capital One (pulse-024). The owner's stated data plans may conflict with written terms (dgn-233). Design owns the access view and the business owns the terms.

position.text: Visa and Mastercard issue no cards and publish their rulebooks, while Discover's and PULSE's operating rules are not public. American Express also issues cards and runs partner issuers and acquirers through its GMNS segment. Capital One reports the network inside Consumer Banking. SHAZAM gives each member institution a vote.

means.text: Name fair-treatment terms for partner issuers, marked as proposals for the business. One term says the owner's bank follows the same operating rules as any issuer. Where law treats the owner's own cards differently, the terms say how. Service levels stay out under the no-timings rule.

Brightline is an acquirer, so the rail can name the owner's debit cards on the network as a reason for its merchants to accept, without claiming lower cost. One rail line can say who reads Brightline's record, including merchant data, since the owner calls direct merchant relationships an attraction of buying a network.
Each partner fact shows who can read it as well as who supplied it. The participant can open a log of the agent's views of its facts.

State data-use terms in plain language beside the API terms, readable without an account, following the pattern of Visa's and Mastercard's public rulebooks. Mark them as a proposal until the business approves them.

objection.text: A Discover executive could object that Discover issued its own credit cards on this network before the sale, and PULSE volume still rose 15% in 2024. Three Discover Debit issuers wrote to the Fed in 2024 backing the deal for better acceptance, competitiveness and equal treatment. Capital One's chief executive said he would love to grow PULSE's business with other banks. A data-separation term would also limit the owner's stated plan to use its data for merchants.

resolution.text: The objection holds on departures, since this study found no public report of a bank leaving PULSE over ownership. The concern is still on record from a Fed commenter, a Datos analyst and a merchant consultancy. In April 2026 the same chief executive said Capital One works back from what would move more of its own business onto the network. The study infers that showing who reads each fact answers the concern without a term the owner has not agreed.

cards.limit: This study found no public report of a bank leaving PULSE or declining Discover over the change of owner. Discover's operating regulations and PULSE's operating rules are not public, so any existing data terms cannot be read (dgn-106, pulse-017). The Fed approval also rests on commitments made to the Board, which this study could not see in full (cross-251). The issuer letters date from 2024, before the close, and the OCC comment file was not read (pulse-078).

cards.title: PULSE states no ATM rate and offers surcharge-free access through Fiserv's MoneyPass, while Discover's map shows no ATM coverage in 15 high-acceptance Caribbean and Central American markets

observed.text: Capital One has substantially completed reissuing legacy debit cards onto the network and advises holders to use Discover or PULSE ATMs in North America and the Caribbean.
NCR Atleos, parent of Cardtronics and Allpoint, says networks set both the interchange issuers pay and the amounts paid to Atleos.
PULSE's ATM pages claim low fees and competitive interchange but state no amount, and Discover's US cash reimbursement schedule sits behind an acquirer code.
PULSE launched its PULSE Select surcharge-free network in 2009 as an alliance with MoneyPass, and its acquirer page now offers a connection to Fiserv's MoneyPass.
Discover's map rates 15 Caribbean and Central American markets 'many locations' for cards, from 2023 to 2025 transaction data, and shows no ATM coverage or bank there.
An Allpoint survey cited by Cardtronics found 53% of retail ATM users chose the machine because it charged no fee.

inference.text: The study infers an ATM owner needs the per-withdrawal rate to plan for network cardholder volume, since networks set what deployers are paid and PULSE states no amount.
The study infers the reissued debit cards may rely on PULSE or Discover at the ATM. Regulation II's two-network rule excludes ATM withdrawals, and Capital One points holders to those marks.
The study infers a deployer joining in the 15 uncovered markets could gain withdrawals from network cardholders, since the map's card ratings come from network transaction data.

decision.question: What should an ATM owner see first when the network courts them?
options: Published earnings per withdrawal, with interchange received and network fees as separate lines and effective dates, beside the traffic the network sends
Traffic first, naming Capital One's reissued debit cardholders, PULSE Select and the 15 uncovered markets, with rates kept for the agreement
Reach claims as PULSE's pages make them now, with rates held for the agreement
decision.evidence_favours: Publishing the economics beside the traffic. NCR Atleos says networks set what deployers are paid, and Visa, Mastercard and Interac publish ATM interchange while PULSE states none (cross-196, visa-467, mastercard-094, interac-013, pulse-085). Rates and any traffic programme are business levers. If rates stay private, the experience can still lead with cited traffic.

position.text: PULSE is behind Visa, Mastercard and Interac on what an ATM owner can read about earnings. All three publish ATM interchange, and Visa and Interac state that the issuer pays the acquirer. Visa prices Plus Alliance surcharge-free withdrawals at a separate rate, and NYCE lets owners choose which machines join SUM. PULSE's surcharge-free access runs through Fiserv's MoneyPass. PULSE offers ATM acquirers exclusive access to Discover, Discover Debit and Diners Club cards.

means.text: For ATM owners, lead with earnings per withdrawal. Publish interchange received and network fees paid as separate lines, and show each change with its effective date, as Interac does.

An ATM owner's home shows earnings per withdrawal beside the surcharge-free withdrawals the network sent to its machines. An ATM acquirer abroad sees network card use in its market where the map shows no ATM coverage.
The ATM Locator API should return the surcharge-free flag that PULSE's public locator already filters on, and show a new operator's machines once live.
Sonia's relationship seat carries the 15 markets with high card acceptance and no ATM bank as a recruitment list for ATM acquirers.

objection.text: Cardtronics says more than 70% of withdrawals at its US ATMs since 2007 ran over Mastercard and Visa. A deployer could argue PULSE's rate barely moves its plans. Cardtronics also alleges PULSE raised its acquirer fees by 200% in 2010, 33% in 2011 and 150% in 2012. A deployer could read a published PULSE rate as a floor for further rises.

resolution.text: The same complaint alleges rises by Exchange, NYCE and STAR in those years, and attributes the pattern to Visa's and Mastercard's access fee rules. Showing the effective date of every change beside the rate answers the fee history. Capital One has reissued about 25 million debit cards onto the network by one trade report, and points holders to Discover and PULSE machines. The study infers a published rate lets a deployer plan for that volume.

cards.limit: What PULSE pays a deployer per withdrawal today is not public. Whether the reissued cards carry another ATM network is not public. Whether PULSE Select still enrols institutions is unclear, since its product page now redirects (pulse-082). The map's levels are qualitative, with no ATM counts. Visa's rule caps an operator's access fee on Visa at its fee on other networks (visa-448). The operators' class action over that rule, certified in 2021, was still in litigation in Visa's FY2025 filing (visa-118).

cards.title: Analysts say a large bank moving card volume off Visa or Mastercard puts incentives at risk, and Discover's owner warns its pricing may fall short

observed.text: Visa recorded 15.75 billion dollars of client incentives in fiscal 2025, and Mastercard recorded 20.5 billion dollars of rebates and incentives in 2025.
Both capitalise up-front incentive payments and amortise them over the contract, with balances of 7.3 billion dollars at Visa and 10.4 billion at Mastercard in 2025.
Discover's owner says rival networks have given issuers large cash signing bonuses, and that Visa's and Mastercard's long-term, sometimes exclusive, bank deals limit its business with those banks.
It warns it may be unable to offer Network Partners adequate pricing while keeping sufficient net revenue.
Discover's unamortised deferred incentive payments were 28 million dollars at the end of 2024, and its 2024 10-K gives no total incentive spend.
On reports that big banks might buy Fiserv's debit networks, a Cornerstone Advisors analyst said Visa would likely reverse such a bank's portfolio discounts. Baird analysts cited lost incentives.

inference.text: The study infers that a large issuer would count incumbent incentives at risk as a switching cost, since two analyst sources and the owner's filing name them.
